items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Stan Kenton, to me, was – I don’t know how to classify him. He always had a good band.

ctx.x: Stan Kenton, to me, was – I don’t know how to classify him. He always had a good band. But to me, Stan Kenton’s band – the trumpet players like Buddy Childers, developed hernia at an early age from playing all those high notes. Shelly Manne used to come home rubbing his hands like a boxer, because he had to roll on a big cymbal as loud as he could, and that wasn’t loud enough. He had to play way over fortissimo. It was a good band, but I wouldn’t say it was – it started to swing when Bill Holman started writing…

We were talking about your career as an author and working in the field of the education of music. I have a book that I don’t know if you were familiar with coming up. I found these probably about 20 years ago in a used book store. It’s called The Science of Drumming, book 1 and 2, by Gene Krupa. Are you familiar with either – with this book?

items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: a thousand musicians can get together and play a chord that Stan Kenton wrote

ctx.x: the great Duke Ellington is taking time out to show me some voicings. Other band leaders have been striving, trying to figure out what did he do there, how did he voice that.

What’s that, I just read a quote from Andre Previn, who said a thousand musicians can get together and play a chord that Stan Kenton wrote and all the arrangers know how to do that. And Duke Ellington writes something for three instruments and they play it and I don’t know what it is.

Well in harmony and in theory it’s really much easier to write for four voices or five voices. But to write for three voices and two voices, because he had three trombone players, and those three trombone players sounded like five or six of them sometimes. But I found after working with the band I discovered in a very short time that you could have Ellington’s band play an arrangement, and then have another choice band, maybe like a New York band or an L.A. band, all great musicians, playing the same chart, but…
